questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Improper Integrals of the Second Kind
questions.problem:
Which of the following is an improper integral of the second kind?

- ${\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{{x}^{2}-9}\,$  II. ${\int }_{-\infty }^{-4}\frac{\text{d}x}{{x}^{2}-9}\,$  III. ${\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{{x}^{2}}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the given integrals.

- Integral I is an improper integral of the second kind since it has finite limits, and 

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-9}\to -\infty \,\text{as}\,x\to {3}^{-}.
$$

- Integral II is an improper integral over an *infinite* domain since its lower limit is infinite.

- Integral III is not an improper integral since it has finite limits and the function under the integral is finite at every point $x\in [1,3].$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

questions.knowledge_point: Rewriting One of the Limits of an Improper Integral
questions.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to 
${\int }_{-1}^{5}\frac{\text{d}x}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded as we approach the *upper* integration limit from any point that lies in the interval $x\in (-1,5):$

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}}\to \infty \,\text{as}\,x\to {5}^{-}
$$

We can attempt to evaluate this integral by integrating $f(x)$ over the interval $x\in [-1,b]$ and taking the limit as $b\to {5}^{-}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{b\to {5}^{-}}({\int }_{-1}^{b}\frac{1}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating an Improper Integral of the Second Kind
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the integral using a substitution. Let $u=x-2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

We use the table below to change the limits:

| $x$ | $2$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $2$ |

Carrying out the change of variable, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{\text{d}x}{x-2} & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{\text{d}u}{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded at the *lower* limit of integration.

$$
f(u)=\frac{1}{u}\to \infty \,\text{ as }\,u\to {0}^{+}.
$$

Nonetheless, it is possible to calculate the integral by setting the *lower* bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to {0}^{+}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{\text{d}u}{u} & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{\int }_{a}^{2}\frac{\text{d}u}{u} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡|u||}_{a}^{2} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}[\operatorname{ln}⁡|2|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|a|] \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{2}{a}| \\  & =\infty \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the integral is divergent.

questions.worked_solution:
This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded at the *lower* limit of integration.

$$
f(x)=\frac{4}{\sqrt[5]{x}}\to \infty \,\text{as}\,x\to {0}^{+}
$$

Nonetheless, it is possible to calculate the integral by setting the *lower* bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to {0}^{+}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{4}{\sqrt[5]{x}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{\int }_{a}^{1}\frac{4}{\sqrt[5]{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{\int }_{a}^{1}4{x}^{-1/5}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}5{x}^{4/5}{|}_{a}^{1} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}5\sqrt[5]{{x}^{4}}{|}_{a}^{1} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}[5\cdot \sqrt[5]{{1}^{4}}-5\cdot \sqrt[5]{{a}^{4}}] \\  & =5(1)-5(0) \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the integral using a substitution. Let $u=3x-2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the table below to change the limits:

| $x$ | $\frac{2}{3}$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $4$ |

Carrying out the change of variable, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2/3}^{2}\frac{3\,\text{d}x}{(3x-2)^{5}} & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{\text{d}u}{{u}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded at the *lower* limit of integration.

$$
f(u)=\frac{1}{{u}^{5}}\to \infty \,\text{ as }\,u\to {0}^{+}.
$$

Nonetheless, it is possible to calculate the integral by setting the *lower* bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to {0}^{+}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{\text{d}u}{{u}^{5}} & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{\int }_{a}^{4}\frac{\text{d}u}{{u}^{5}} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{\int }_{a}^{4}{u}^{-5}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{(-\frac{1}{4}\,{u}^{-4})|}_{a}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{\frac{1}{{u}^{4}}|}_{a}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}[\frac{1}{256}-\frac{1}{{a}^{4}}] \\  & =\infty \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the integral is divergent.

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating an Improper Integral of the Second Kind
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the integral using a substitution. Let $u=4-t.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=-1\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\text{d}t.
$$

We use the table below to change the limits:

| $t$ | $1$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $3$ | $0$ |

Carrying out the change of variable, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{\text{d}t}{\sqrt{4-t}} & ={\int }_{3}^{0}\frac{-\text{d}u}{\sqrt{u}} \\  & =-{\int }_{3}^{0}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{u}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{u}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded at the *lower* limit of integration.

$$
f(u)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\to \infty \,\text{ as }\,u\to {0}^{+}.
$$

Nonetheless, it is possible to calculate the integral by setting the *lower* bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to {0}^{+}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{u}} & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{\int }_{a}^{3}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{u}} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{\int }_{a}^{3}{u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{2{u}^{1/2}|}_{a}^{3} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{2\sqrt{u}|}_{a}^{3} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}[2\sqrt{3}-2\sqrt{a}] \\  & =2\sqrt{3}-0 \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{\text{d}t}{\sqrt{4-t}}=2\sqrt{3}.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the integral using a substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,⟹\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

We use the table below to change the limits:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Carrying out the change of variable, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\sqrt[5]{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt[5]{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{-1/5}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded at the *lower* limit of integration.

$$
f(u)={u}^{-1/5}\to \infty \,\text{ as }\,u\to {0}^{+}.
$$

Nonetheless, it is possible to calculate the integral by setting the *lower* bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to {0}^{+}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{-1/5}\,\text{d}u & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{\int }_{a}^{1}{u}^{-1/5}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{\frac{5}{4}{u}^{4/5}|}_{a}^{1} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}[\frac{5}{4}\cdot {1}^{4/5}-\frac{5}{4}\cdot {a}^{4/5}] \\  & =\frac{5}{4}-0 \\  & =\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\sqrt[5]{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{5}{4}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following is an improper integral of the second kind?

- $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{x-2}\qquad$  II. $\displaystyle \int_{-2}^{0} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{x+2}\qquad$  III. $\displaystyle \int_{2}^{3} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{x^2-1}$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the given integrals.

- Integral I is an improper integral over an *infinite* domain since its upper limit is infinite. So, it is not an improper integral of the second kind.

- Integral II is an improper integral of the second kind since it has finite limits, and 

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x+2} \rightarrow \infty \quad \textrm{as}\quad x\rightarrow (-2)^+.
$$

- Integral III is not an improper integral since it has finite limits, and the function under the integral is finite at every point $x\in[2,3].$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

canonical_examples.problem: Rewrite the improper integral $\displaystyle {\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{x^2-1}}$ as the limit of definite integral.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded as we approach the *upper* integration limit from any point that lies in the interval $x\in (0,{\color{blue}{1}})\mathbin{:}$

$$
f(x) =   \dfrac {1}{x^2-1} \rightarrow -\infty\quad \textrm{as}\quad x\rightarrow {\color{blue}{1}} ^-
$$

We can attempt to evaluate this integral by integrating $f(x)$ over the interval $x\in [0, b]$ and taking the limit as $b\to{\color{blue}1}^-\mathbin{:}$

$$
\displaystyle {\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{x^2-1}} = \lim\limits_{b \to {\color{blue}{1}}^-} \left( \displaystyle {\int_{0}^{b} \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{x^2-1}}   \right)
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating an Improper Integral of the Second Kind
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the integral using a substitution. Let $u = \cos x.$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -\sin x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad -\textrm d u = \sin x\,\textrm d x.
$$

We use the table below to change the limits:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $0$ |

Carrying out the change of variable, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{0}\frac{-\text{d}u}{u} \\  & =-{\int }_{1}^{0}\frac{\text{d}u}{u} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\text{d}u}{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded at the *lower* limit of integration.

$$
f(u) = \dfrac{1}{u} \rightarrow \infty \quad\textrm{ as }\quad u\rightarrow 0^+.
$$

Nonetheless, it is possible to calculate the integral by setting the *lower* bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to0^+.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\text{d}u}{u} & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{\int }_{a}^{1}\frac{\text{d}u}{u} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡|u||}_{a}^{1} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}[\operatorname{ln}⁡|1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|a|] \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}[0-\operatorname{ln}⁡|a|] \\  & =-(-\infty ) \\  & =\infty \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the integral is divergent.
